stages.title: Atomic structure and electron configurations
stages.hook: Sodium and potassium both react fiercely with water, but neon and argon barely react with anything. What inside the atom explains this?
explain: An atom has a tiny dense nucleus made of protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge). Electrons (negative) move around the nucleus. The atomic number is the number of protons. The mass number is protons plus neutrons. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14. Both have 6 protons. The relative atomic mass on the periodic table is a weighted average of the isotopes.

Electrons occupy shells at increasing distances. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second and third up to 8 each (for the first 20 elements). Sodium (11 electrons) is 2,8,1 and chlorine (17) is 2,8,7. The outer-shell electrons decide how an element reacts, and a full outer shell, as in neon (2,8), means very little reactivity.

example.q: Write the electron configuration of magnesium (atomic number 12).
steps: Fill shell 2 with 8, leaving 2 for shell 3.

stages.title: Stoichiometry and mole calculations
stages.hook: A recipe says '2 eggs per cake'. How can chemists count atoms when they are too tiny to see, and weigh them instead?
explain: Chemists count particles in moles. One mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). The molar mass, in g/mol, is the mass of one mole and equals the relative formula mass. Using H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Cl 35.5: water H₂O is 18 g/mol, CO₂ is 44 g/mol and NaCl is 58.5 g/mol.
The key formula is moles = mass ÷ molar mass, so mass = moles × molar mass. For a solution, moles = concentration (mol/L) × volume (L).

A balanced equation gives mole ratios. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 mol H₂ react with 1 mol O₂ to give 2 mol H₂O. So we convert mass to moles, use the ratio, then convert back to mass. This is stoichiometry.

example.q: How many grams of water form from 4 g of hydrogen in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O? (H 1, O 16)
steps: Ratio H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2, so 2 mol water.

stages.title: Ionic and covalent bonding
stages.hook: Table salt melts at about 800 °C but sugar breaks down much more easily, and water boils at 100 °C. Why such a difference?
explain: Ionic bonding happens between metals and non-metals. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positive ions and non-metals gain electrons to become negative ions. Sodium (2,8,1) loses 1 electron to become Na⁺ and chlorine (2,8,7) gains 1 to become Cl⁻. Magnesium loses 2 to form Mg²⁺, so magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.
The strong attraction between ions in a giant lattice makes ionic compounds hard, brittle, high-melting and able to conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because then the ions can move.

Covalent bonding is between non-metals. Atoms share pairs of electrons to fill their outer shells. Water has two single bonds, oxygen gas has a double bond and nitrogen gas a triple bond. Small covalent molecules have weak forces between molecules, so they usually have low melting and boiling points.

example.q: What is the formula of the compound of calcium (Ca²⁺) and chloride (Cl⁻)?
steps: Need two Cl⁻ to balance one Ca²⁺.

stages.title: Molecular geometry
stages.hook: Water has the formula H₂O but its three atoms are not in a straight line. Why do molecules have particular shapes?
explain: Electron pairs around a central atom repel each other, so they spread out as far apart as possible. This is the idea behind VSEPR theory. The shape depends on how many bonding pairs and lone pairs surround the central atom.

Four bonding pairs, as in methane CH₄, give a tetrahedral shape with bond angles about 109.5°. Ammonia NH₃ has three bonding pairs and one lone pair, giving a pyramid shape with angles about 107°. Water has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs and is bent, about 104.5°. Carbon dioxide has two double bonds and is linear, 180°.

Lone pairs push harder than bonding pairs, so angles shrink. Shape matters because it decides whether a molecule is polar: bent water is polar, while linear CO₂ is not, since its two polar bonds cancel.

example.q: Predict the shape of BF₃, which has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
steps: Three electron pairs spread as far apart as possible.
They lie in a flat plane.

stages.title: Reaction balancing
stages.hook: Methane burns: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Count the atoms on each side. Why doesn't this equation work yet?
explain: A balanced equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, because atoms are not created or destroyed. We balance by changing the big numbers (coefficients) in front of formulas, never the small subscripts.

Method: write the correct formulas; count atoms of each element on each side; adjust coefficients one element at a time, leaving oxygen or hydrogen for last; recheck all counts. For methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Left: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. Right: 1 C, 4 H, 2 + 2 = 4 O. Balanced.
State symbols show the physical state: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water. Balanced equations are the starting point for mole calculations.

steps: Left has 2 N, so we need 2 NH₃ on the right: N₂ + H₂ → 2NH₃.
Right now has 6 H, so we need 3 H₂ on the left.
Check: left 2 N, 6 H; right 2 N, 6 H.

stages.title: Thermochemistry
stages.hook: A hand warmer gets hot and an instant cold pack gets cold, yet both are just chemical changes. What is energy doing?
explain: Chemical reactions involve energy changes. Breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds releases energy. If more energy is released than taken in, the reaction is exothermic and heats its surroundings. If more is taken in, it is endothermic and cools them.

The enthalpy change ΔH is the heat change at constant pressure. It is negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic reactions. For example, burning methane has ΔH of about −890 kJ per mole of methane.

Heat absorbed by water or a solution is found from q = m × c × ΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity (4.18 J/g°C for water), m is the mass in grams and ΔT is the temperature change. This is how calorimetry works.

example.q: A reaction heats 100 g of water by 5.0 °C. How much heat did the water gain? (c = 4.18 J/g°C)

stages.title: Reaction rates and catalysts
stages.hook: A whole potato takes ages to cook but chips cook in minutes. What can speed up or slow down a reaction?
explain: The rate of a reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products form. We can measure it as change in concentration (or mass or volume of gas) divided by time. For example, if a concentration falls from 0.50 to 0.20 mol/L in 30 s, the average rate is 0.30 ÷ 30 = 0.010 mol/L/s.

Collision theory says particles must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) and in the right orientation. Higher temperature makes particles move faster and collide harder and more often. Higher concentration or pressure means more collisions. Smaller pieces (more surface area) expose more particles.

A catalyst speeds up a reaction by giving a path with lower activation energy. It is not used up. Enzymes are biological catalysts. Catalysts do not change the products or the energy released overall.

example.q: Why does powdered chalk react faster with acid than a big lump?
steps: Powder has a much larger surface area.
More particles are exposed to the acid.
So more collisions per second and a faster rate.

stages.title: Chemical equilibrium
stages.hook: In a sealed bottle of fizzy drink, carbon dioxide dissolves and escapes at the same time. Why does the bubble level look unchanged?
explain: Some reactions are reversible and can go both ways, shown by ⇌. In a closed system the forward and backward reactions eventually go at the same rate. This is dynamic equilibrium: the amounts stay constant but both reactions keep going.
At equilibrium we can write the equilibrium constant Kc. For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). A large Kc means products are favoured. Kc depends only on temperature.

Le Chatelier's principle says that if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to oppose the change. Adding reactant shifts it to the products. Raising pressure shifts to the side with fewer gas molecules. Heating favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not shift the position.

example.q: For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at equilibrium, [H₂] = 0.10, [I₂] = 0.10, [HI] = 0.40 mol/L. Find Kc.

stages.title: Materials classification and mechanical properties
stages.hook: A steel bridge bends slightly under a truck and springs back, but a glass plate shatters with almost no bending. How do we measure and compare such behaviour?
explain: Materials are classed as metals, ceramics, polymers and composites. Metals are strong and ductile and conduct heat and electricity. Ceramics are hard, brittle and heat resistant. Polymers are light and flexible with low melting points. Composites combine two materials, like fibreglass or reinforced concrete, to get the best of both.

Stress is force per unit area: σ = F ÷ A, in pascals (Pa, 1 Pa = 1 N/m²). Strain is the fractional change in length: ε = ΔL ÷ L, with no units. For small loads the two are proportional, which is elastic behaviour. The ratio stress ÷ strain is the Young's modulus E, a measure of stiffness.

Elastic means the material returns to its shape when the load is removed. Beyond the yield point it deforms plastically and stays deformed. Strength is the stress at failure, hardness resists scratching and indentation, ductile materials stretch and brittle materials snap with little stretch.

analogies.home: A rubber band stretches and returns (elastic) but a paper clip bent too far stays bent (plastic).
analogies.sport: A diving board bends and springs back; a cricket bat crack is brittle failure.
analogies.city: Bridges use steel for strength, pipes use polymers, bricks are ceramics.
analogies.farm: A wire fence stretches a little under a push; dry twigs snap.

misc.wrong: A strong material is the same as a stiff one.
misc.right: Strength is the stress at failure and stiffness is resistance to elastic stretching, which is a different property.

stages.limits: Real materials differ from the simple linear model, especially polymers and near the yield point.
